explainBack.question: Why could cancelling Pro $200 today lock you out of the tier tomorrow, even though OpenAI says existing subscribers are unaffected?
explainBack.answer: Because the pause blocks entry, not continuation. While your subscription is active it renews as usual — that is the 'unaffected' part. But once a cancellation, completed downgrade, or failed renewal actually ends the plan, you no longer hold an active subscription; buying Pro $200 again would count as a new sign-up, and new sign-ups are exactly what OpenAI paused. So the same account is protected one day and blocked the next, depending on whether the change has taken effect.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: A correct answer must distinguish an active subscription (renews, P003/P004) from an ended one (repurchase blocked until the pause lifts, P004), and note the scheduled-vs-effective timing boundary (P006).
explainBack.assessment: The article supplies every link in this chain explicitly, so a reader can reproduce this causal answer in ordinary language; the mechanism is complete and accurate.

unseenTransfer.scenario: A music-streaming service announces a capacity-driven pause on new sign-ups to its top 'Lossless Max' tier. Dana subscribes to that tier but wants to drop to the cheap tier for two months while travelling, planning to switch back afterwards.
unseenTransfer.question: Using the article's mechanism, should Dana treat the temporary downgrade as safely reversible?
unseenTransfer.answer: No. The article's mechanism says a sign-up pause protects only a continuously active subscription; any change that takes effect ends that protection. Once Dana's downgrade completes, returning to Lossless Max is a new upgrade into a paused tier, blocked until the pause lifts — and no restart date is promised. Dana should check the service's official pause policy for the scheduled-vs-effective rule before confirming, because a scheduled change may still leave the tier active through the current billing cycle.
